intro:
The exercises in this chapter all circle one decision: for every function you write, what is the smallest runtime surface it can honestly tolerate? The three-ring model (core always available, alloc requiring a heap, std requiring an operating system) is the lens. The warm-up exercise establishes that vocabulary, the code-reading exercise traces the fixed-capacity Pool that makes the model concrete, and the implementation exercises push you to keep the baseline API slice-based, encode peripheral ownership with move semantics, and convert an infallible allocation into a fallible one that returns out-of-memory to the caller.

The payoff is a single crate that ships unchanged to four very different homes: firmware on a sensor board, kernel-adjacent hypervisor startup code, a sandboxed wasm guest, and an ordinary server. Getting there is less about exotic syntax than about refusing the hosted-programming reflexes that assume an allocator, a panic printer, or an unwinder always exist. The design exercise and the lab tie the pieces together: a feature-gated surface whose runtime contract is stated explicitly per target.

exerciseSolutions.title: Place each function at its lowest ring
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Read the standard library as three stacked layers and no_std as opting out of the upper ones. The capability each ring asks of the target is distinct. The core ring is the language itself plus pure types and operations; it requires nothing of the target and is therefore always available regardless of target triple. The alloc ring requires a heap, that is, a working global allocator, because everything it offers (Vec, Box, String, BTreeMap) owns growable memory. The std ring requires an operating system underneath, because it layers files, threads, sockets, environment, time, and a default panic strategy on top of alloc.

Now pin each function from the crate root. checksum(bytes: &[u8]) -> u32 takes a borrowed slice and returns an integer. It never owns memory and never calls the OS, so the single concrete need is nothing beyond the language: it lives in core and compiles everywhere. encode_frame(tag, payload) -> Vec<u8> returns an owned, growable Vec<u8>. The one concrete need is a heap to grow that buffer, which is exactly the alloc ring, so it sits behind the alloc feature. write_diagnostic(service, checksum) -> String produces a host-facing String through format! and is meant for diagnostics on a hosted system; its concrete need is the OS-backed std machinery, so it sits behind the std feature.

no_std and no-heap are two separate decisions because they target two different layers. no_std removes only the top layer (std); the heap belongs to the alloc layer below it. A crate can be #![no_std] and still write extern crate alloc; and use Vec, Box, and String freely, as long as the final binary supplies a global allocator. So dropping std does not by itself remove the heap; you make the second, independent choice of whether to use alloc on top of core. Finally, the target triple decides the highest ring a given build is allowed to reach: a bare-metal triple may stop at core (or core plus a hand-wired allocator for alloc), a wasm guest typically reaches alloc, and a server triple reaches all the way to std.
criteria: States core is always available, alloc requires a heap (a global allocator), and std requires an OS.

Pins checksum to core (slice in, integer out), encode_frame to alloc (returns an owned Vec<u8>), and write_diagnostic to std (formats host-facing diagnostics, returning a String, for an environment with an OS).
Explains a crate can be no_std yet use alloc, so dropping std does not remove the heap.
Identifies the target triple as what determines the highest ring a build may use.

exerciseSolutions.title: Trace the fixed-capacity Pool
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Example 2 defines Pool<const SLOTS, const BYTES> with three parallel fixed arrays: used: [bool; SLOTS] tracks occupancy, lens: [usize; SLOTS] records the byte length stored per slot, and data: [[u8; BYTES]; SLOTS] is the backing storage. Nothing here is heap-allocated; SLOTS bounds how many buffers exist and BYTES bounds the size of each one, both at compile time.

Walk alloc_copy. It first checks if bytes.len() > BYTES and returns None when the input is too large for a single slot. Otherwise it scans slots from index 0, and at the first slot whose used flag is false it sets used[index] = true, records lens[index] = bytes.len(), copies the bytes in with copy_from_slice, and returns Some(SlotId(index)). If the loop finishes without finding a free slot, it returns None. So alloc_copy returns None on oversize input, and otherwise returns None only when every slot is already used; on success it returns Some(SlotId).

Now trace Pool::<2, 8>. The first allocation of b"abc" (length 3, well under BYTES = 8) takes slot 0. The second allocation of b"rust" (length 4) takes slot 1. The third allocation of b"more" (length 4) fails: 4 is not greater than BYTES, so the byte check passes, but both of the two slots are now occupied, so the scan finds nothing free and returns None. That is why overflow is true, and it fails because the pool is out of slots, not out of per-slot bytes. sent_bytes is computed before the release as pool.as_slice(first).len(), and as_slice returns &data[id.0][..lens[id.0]], so its length is lens[0] = 3, the length of b"abc". Then pool.release(first) sets used[0] = false and lens[0] = 0, which is exactly what makes the slot reusable: clearing the used flag frees it and zeroing the recorded length means a future as_slice on that index yields an empty slice until something is written again. After release, in_use counts the still-used flags, which is just slot 1, so in_use = 1. The program therefore prints in_use = 1, overflow = true, sent bytes = 3.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Hand-trace of Example 2's Pool::<2, 8>, predicting each printed value without running it.
criteria: Shows alloc_copy returns None when bytes.len() exceeds BYTES, and otherwise None only when every slot is used.
Explains the third allocation fails because both slots are occupied, not because of byte capacity.
Computes in_use = 1 after release, overflow = true, and sent_bytes = 3 (length of b"abc"), printed in the order in_use, overflow, sent_bytes to match Example 2's println! order.
Identifies release as clearing the used flag and zeroing lens for the slot so it can be reused.

exerciseSolutions.title: Keep checksum slice-based across every ring
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The whole point of taking a borrowed slice is portability. An array literal on a sensor board, a wasm guest buffer, and a Vec<u8> on a server all coerce to &[u8], so a function over &[u8] serves every caller without owning anything. Keep the signature exactly fn checksum(bytes: &[u8]) -> u32 and do the reduction as a single iterator chain: map each byte widened to u32, then sum.

Widening to u32 before summing matters for correctness, not just types. If you summed in u8 you would wrap at 256; folding each byte into a u32 accumulator gives the true total. checksum(b"abc") is 97 + 98 + 99 = 294, which matches the lab's expected checksum. The body constructs no intermediate Vec or String; iter() borrows, map yields values, and sum() folds into a single u32 register-width accumulator.

Nothing in the body forces the alloc or std ring. There is no Vec, Box, String, or format!, no file or thread or socket, no panic path that depends on std (an empty slice simply sums to 0). The function therefore compiles at the core ring and is usable identically on a freestanding firmware target, inside a wasm guest, and on a hosted server. The call sites below show the same function accepting both an array literal and &vec[..] from a Vec<u8>, demonstrating that the slice signature is what lets one function span all three rings.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: checksum over a borrowed slice, plus call sites from an array and a Vec<u8> proving one function spans every ring.
criteria: Signature stays fn checksum(bytes: &[u8]) -> u32 and takes a borrowed slice, not an owned Vec.
Body widens each byte to u32 and sums without building a new Vec or String.
No alloc or std type appears, so the function belongs at the core ring.
checksum(b"abc") returns 294 and the same function accepts &vec[..] from a Vec<u8>.

exerciseSolutions.title: Transfer slot ownership to a DMA handoff
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Close to the hardware, ownership stops being about cleanup and becomes a tool for reasoning about who is physically allowed to touch memory at a given instant. A DMA engine is a concurrent actor you cannot see from ordinary code: once you hand it a buffer, it may read or write that buffer at any time until the transfer completes. The design encodes that fact in the type system so the caller is structurally unable to touch the buffer while the transfer is in flight.

Define SlotId as the token that represents the right to access one slot, and a separate InFlight type that wraps the moved SlotId. submit_to_dma(slot: SlotId) -> InFlight takes the SlotId by value, which moves it. After the call the caller's original SlotId binding is gone, so there is no path by which the caller can read or write the buffer. complete(token: InFlight) -> SlotId consumes the InFlight token by value and returns the original SlotId, restoring access only once the transfer has finished. The peripheral conceptually owns the memory for the entire interval between submit and complete.

The reason a use of the slot between submit and complete is a compile error rather than a runtime race is move semantics, not any runtime check or atomic. The SlotId was moved into submit_to_dma; the original binding is no longer live, so referring to it does not type-check. There is no flag to poll, no lock to forget, and no window where two actors hold the slot at once. The exclusivity is proven at compile time and costs nothing at run time. The token chain (SlotId -> InFlight -> SlotId) makes the handoff and the return of ownership both explicit and unforgeable.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Move-based DMA handoff: SlotId -> InFlight -> SlotId makes touching the buffer mid-transfer a compile error.
criteria: submit_to_dma takes slot: SlotId by value and returns an InFlight that owns it.
complete takes the InFlight token by value and returns the original SlotId.
Using the moved SlotId after submit_to_dma fails to compile (E0382), shown in the commented line.
Write-up names move semantics, not a runtime check or atomic, as what enforces exclusive access.

exerciseSolutions.title: Replace an infallible push with try_reserve
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is an unspoken assumption that allocation always succeeds. The original encoder calls out.extend_from_slice(payload) directly. On a hosted system an allocation failure inside extend_from_slice aborts the process, which is tolerable because the OS reclaims everything and a server restart is cheap. On a constrained target there is a fixed memory budget and growth can genuinely fail, and an abort there takes down the whole firmware image with no operator to restart it. Out-of-memory has to become a value the caller can handle, not a process abort.

The fix is one method plus a changed return type. Make the function return Result<Vec<u8>, TryReserveError> so the failure is visible in the signature. Call out.try_reserve(needed) for the exact capacity you are about to add and propagate its error with ?. try_reserve returns Result<(), TryReserveError>, so ? converts a reservation failure straight into the function's error. Crucially, reserve capacity first and only extend once the reservation has succeeded. That ordering is what guarantees no bytes are written on the failure path: if try_reserve returns Err, the function returns before any extend_from_slice runs, and the buffer is left untouched.

The reason this matters is the difference between hosted and constrained failure semantics. On a hosted target an allocation abort is an acceptable last resort. On a constrained target the same abort is a denial-of-service against the device, so the design question shifts from "how do I allocate?" to "what happens when I cannot?" Returning the out-of-memory case as an Err keeps the encoder honest about its runtime contract and lets the caller back off, drop the frame, or signal upstream instead of crashing.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: encode_frame returns Result<Vec<u8>, TryReserveError>: try_reserve up front, extend only after capacity is secured.
criteria: Returns a Result whose error path is a failed reservation rather than an abort.
Calls try_reserve and propagates its error with ? before any push or extend_from_slice.
No bytes are written on the failure path because the early return precedes every write.
Explanation notes allocation can genuinely fail on constrained targets, so OOM must be a handled value, not a process abort.

exerciseSolutions.title: Ship one framing library across four homes
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Design the smallest truthful API first, then layer conveniences only where a product boundary genuinely benefits. The crate is #![no_std] by default. The checksum surface (slice in, integer out) lives in core, because it needs nothing but the language and so compiles on all four targets unchanged. The frame-encode surface, which returns an owned, growable Vec<u8>, sits behind the alloc feature, because owning a growable buffer is exactly the capability the alloc ring adds. The host-diagnostic surface, which builds a String for human-readable logging, sits behind the std feature, because it is meant for a hosted system and pulls in OS-backed machinery. That split matches the shape the chapter recommends: slice-based core, alloc-gated owned helpers, std-gated host diagnostics.

Each target imposes a runtime contract for whatever std would otherwise have supplied. The bare-metal firmware is freestanding: the release contract must include an explicit #[panic_handler], a chosen allocator if the alloc feature is on, startup glue (reset vector and the code that runs before main), and a linker script that places sections in the board's memory map. The hypervisor startup code is kernel-adjacent and similarly freestanding: it needs an explicit panic policy and startup glue, must avoid assuming an unwinder exists at the ABI seam, and typically runs without a heap until one is wired up. The wasm guest talks to the host over a narrow ABI: it usually reaches the alloc ring, but panic and allocation policy must stay explicit at the boundary because the host cannot safely consume an implicit unwind or an unexpected heap contract. The server is the only target that reaches std and gets the panic handler, allocator, and startup for free.

For the firmware path, prefer both fixed-capacity slots and fallible allocation rather than assuming infallible allocation. Where the bounds are real (a known maximum number of in-flight frames, a known maximum frame size), a fixed-capacity Pool with bounded slots is the strongest choice: it cannot fail at run time for lack of heap because there is no heap involved, and it makes the memory budget visible in the type. Where dynamic growth is genuinely required, use try_reserve so out-of-memory is returned as a value rather than aborting the image. Both make the failure mode explicit instead of hoping an allocator never says no.

Finally, separate host-side std tests from target-specific harnesses so the fast tests stay fast. The portable core logic (checksum, frame layout, slot bookkeeping) is just data transformation and can be exercised with ordinary std tests, fuzzers, and property tests on the developer's machine, which run in milliseconds. Target-specific behavior (the real panic handler firing, MMIO, DMA completion, the wasm ABI) is validated separately on emulators or hardware, which is slower. Keeping the two apart means the bulk of the logic is covered by the fast suite, and the slow device or guest harnesses only have to confirm the genuinely target-dependent behavior.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Feature-gated crate surface: core checksum, alloc-gated encode_frame, std-gated write_diagnostic, with the per-ring Cargo features.
criteria: Smallest truthful API is slice-based in core, owned helpers are alloc-gated, host diagnostics are std-gated.
Names the freestanding targets' contract: explicit panic handler, allocator choice, startup glue, and linker script.
Firmware path prefers fixed-capacity slots plus fallible allocation over assuming infallible allocation.
Portable core logic is tested on the host with std while target-specific behavior is validated separately to keep fast tests fast.

labSolution.explanation:
FramePool models the chapter's fixed-capacity Pool in plain std: a bounded number of slots, each backed by a Vec<u8>, where allocation can fail. The pool here has two slots and a per-slot capacity of eight bytes. The completed alloc_copy first rejects any input longer than self.capacity by returning None, then scans for the first slot whose used flag is false, claims it, clears the slot's buffer, copies the bytes in with extend_from_slice, and returns Some(index). If no slot is free it returns None.

The main routine drives the three printed values. alloc_copy(b"abc") (length 3, within capacity 8) takes slot 0, so first is 0. alloc_copy(b"rust") (length 4) takes slot 1. alloc_copy(b"overflowing") is length 11, which is greater than the capacity of 8, so it is rejected by the length check and returns None, making overflow true. first_sum is checksum of slot 0's bytes, b"abc", which is 97 + 98 + 99 = 294. Then pool.release(first) frees slot 0, leaving only slot 1 occupied, so in_use returns 1.

That produces exactly checksum = 294, overflow = true, in_use = 1. Note that overflow here is driven by per-slot byte capacity (the 11-byte input does not fit a single 8-byte slot), whereas in Example 2's two-slot trace the overflow came from running out of slots. Both are the same lesson: on a bounded pool, allocation is fallible and the caller must handle the None.

reviewAnswers.question: What capability does each of the three rings require of a target, and which ring is always available regardless of target triple?
reviewAnswers.answer: core requires nothing of the target beyond the language itself; it provides pure types and operations and is always available regardless of target triple. alloc requires a heap, that is, a working global allocator, because it provides owned, growable types such as Vec, Box, and String. std requires an operating system underneath, because it layers files, threads, sockets, time, environment access, and a default panic strategy on top of alloc.

reviewAnswers.question: Why are no_std and no-heap two independent decisions rather than one, and how does the alloc feature relate to that distinction?
reviewAnswers.answer: no_std removes only the top layer, std; the heap lives in the alloc layer below it, so removing std does not by itself remove the heap. A crate can be #![no_std] and still pull in alloc to use Vec, Box, and String, provided the final binary supplies a global allocator. The alloc feature is exactly the switch for that second, independent decision: keep the language-only core surface, or opt back into heap-owning types without taking on all of std.

reviewAnswers.question: On a freestanding target, why does the compiler require you to supply a #[panic_handler], and what does std normally provide in its place?
reviewAnswers.answer: On a hosted target, std supplies a default panic handler for free: it prints a message and then unwinds or aborts using OS-backed machinery. A freestanding target has no std and no OS to do that, so the compiler cannot fall back on a default and requires you to provide a #[panic_handler] yourself. That handler defines the panic policy explicitly, for example halting the core or spinning forever, making panic strategy a first-class item you own rather than a background detail.

reviewAnswers.question: How does taking a slot by value in a submit_to_dma-style API turn a potential data race with a DMA engine into a compile-time error?
reviewAnswers.answer: Taking the slot by value moves it into submit_to_dma, which returns an InFlight handle that now owns it; the caller's original binding is dead. Because the slot was moved, any attempt to read or write that buffer while the transfer is in flight fails to type-check, since the value no longer exists in the caller's scope. Ownership returns only when complete consumes the InFlight token and hands the slot back, so exclusivity during the transfer is enforced by move semantics at compile time, with no runtime flag, lock, or atomic involved.

reviewAnswers.question: What does try_reserve change about a buffer-growing function compared with calling push or extend_from_slice directly, and why does that matter on a constrained target?
reviewAnswers.answer: try_reserve attempts to secure capacity and returns Result<(), TryReserveError>, so an allocation failure becomes a value the function can propagate to the caller; a direct push or extend_from_slice instead aborts the process on failure. Reserving up front and only extending after the reservation succeeds also means the buffer is left untouched on the failure path. This matters on a constrained target because memory is a fixed budget and growth can genuinely fail, and an abort would take down the whole firmware image, so out-of-memory must be a handled error rather than a process abort.
